# Egashira et al., TestSuiteBench: generating test suites from specifications

**Source:** Egashira, Mündler-Sasahara, Müller and Vechev (ETH Zurich; LogicStar.ai), *TestSuiteBench: Coding Agents Struggle to Generate Strong Test Suites from Specifications*, preprint, arXiv:2610.13065v1 [cs.SE], 9 Oct 2026, 25 pages. CC BY 4.0.
**Structure:** a benchmark paper: the verification gap (§1), construction and metrics (§2, App. B, D.1), experiments (§3, App. A, C, D.2), related work (§4), limitations (§5), conclusion (§6), reproducibility and AI-usage statements, and a list of all 165 instances (App. E).

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

Coding agents have gone from resolving isolated issues to re-implementing complex applications, which suggests fully autonomous development of new software is within reach. The authors argue it depends on strong verification against intended behaviour: re-implementations can lean on existing test suites and reference implementations, but new software starts with only a natural-language specification, so the agent must turn that specification into a strong test suite. Existing test-generation benchmarks do not measure this, being limited to issues, a few files or single scenarios and always providing the implementation (§1, "Introduction").

TestSuiteBench gives an agent only the specification and scores the suite it writes by validity (the share of its tests that pass on the reference implementation) and mutation score (the share of requirement-targeted mutants its valid tests kill). Across agents on six frontier models, the best suite (Claude Opus 5) kills 55.5% of mutants, four of six stay below 40%, yet four of six write tests that are 88-96% valid and implementations from the same specifications pass up to 93% of reference tests. The authors conclude that agents can build software they cannot verify, that the bottleneck is test design rather than specification precision, and that generated suites are often too small and miss the input combinations needed to expose violated requirements (Abstract; §1; §3.1; §6).

## The benchmark and how it was built

The starting point is an existing benchmark of 200 open-source command-line programs with compiled executables and extensive pure input-output test suites [BT]. Filtering out tests that need internet access, need excessive resources or are flaky on the reference leaves 165 instances, with reference suites 5.7% smaller on average (§2.1; App. B.1). An agent writes a draft specification describing every tested behaviour in 10 to 50 sections, as an abstracted description rather than a list of test functions (§2.1; App. D.1).

The mutants are the core: each targets one test chosen so that the six targets per section cover the specification evenly (solved as a min-cost flow), and an agent edits the reference so only that test kills it. Refinement keeps the best three per section and drops any mutant its target misses or that over 20% of unrelated tests kill, raising the share killed exactly by the target from 32.4% to 73.0% and cutting other killers from 1.45% to 0.17% on average. The prompts ask for a rule "a re-implementer could plausibly get wrong" across an input class, and forbid hard-coding the target test's literals (§2.2; App. B.2; App. D.1). The specification is then refined in a loop: trial agents build an implementation and a suite from it, each failure is attributed to a bad generation or to a specification defect (underspecification or contradiction), affected sections are fixed, and the loop stops when under 5% of generated-test failures are blamed on the specification (§2.3). Manual review fixed 34 instances, 20 of them where the specification gave an exact error location that let every mutant be killed by one test (§2.4; App. B.3).

## Metrics and setup

The mutation score M counts mutants killed by the valid tests; tests failing on the reference are filtered out first, and suites run three times on the reference with tests that change behaviour removed. The validity rate V is the share of generated tests that pass on the reference, and the reference pass rate R scores generated implementations against the reference suite. Agents run in containers without networking and with search tools disabled, to prevent cheating (§2.6). The finished benchmark is 165 Rust, Go and C/C++ programs, with a median specification of about 5k words in 23 sections, 679 reference tests and 67 mutants (§2.5; Table 1). Agents ran with vendor-recommended harnesses under a 6-hour limit, and the prompt told them how scoring works and asked for at least one meaningful test per documented behaviour (§3; App. C; App. D.2).

## Main results

Claude Opus 5 leads at 55.5% M ($10.56, 37 min per instance), then GPT 6 Astra at 50.1% ($2.18); Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT 5.6 Sol, DeepSeek V4 Flash and GPT 5.6 Luna score 37.9%, 37.7%, 28.6% and 19.3%. The table's caption puts it as agents failing to reach M beyond 56% even when V and R are almost 100% (Table 2; §3.1). The authors read high V and R as showing the specifications convey the expected behaviour, which makes the weak suites a capability gap; valid tests give "the impression of well tested software" while missing specification violations, which they say matches commonly observed agent behaviour, without a citation (§3.1).

Cost and M have a clear logarithmic relationship, with more spending giving marginal gains; GPT 5.6 Sol's M rises from 31.3% on low reasoning effort ($0.45) to 46.5% on xhigh ($2.4) (§3.1; Figure 5).

## Why the suites are weak

All models write smaller suites than the reference: Opus by 8.9%, Sol by about five times. M tends to be better where there are fewer requirements and more generated tests, and correlates weakly and negatively with specification sections (§3.2; Figure 6; App. A.1-A.2). Opus built executables in 149 instances and mutants in 33 while writing tests; Sol built almost none yet beat DeepSeek, so the authors judge such scaffolding not necessary (§3.2; Table 3). The error analysis finds core functionality tested while input combinations and edge cases are left out: a suite that tests a search command on one file misses a mutant that ignores the second; a completion test checks only that the output is long and mentions commands, so a wrong shell's script passes (§3.2; App. A.6).

Two ablations bound the explanation. Giving Sol the reference executable raised V from 94.4% to 98.4% but left M at 38.1% against 37.7%, so ambiguity does not explain low scores (§3.2; Table 4). On 30 instances, swapping the benchmark specification for developer documentation cut Sol's M from 25.5% to 4.0%, with 40% fewer tests, lower validity and three times the underspecification failures per test (§3.2; Table 5). Pooling the suites of Opus, Sol and Gemini raises the killed share only from 54% (Opus alone) to 59%, leaving 41% that no model kills; only 25% are killed by all three (App. A.5).

## Limits the authors state

Mutants are a proxy: they sample requirements, each violates one requirement by design, and they need not reflect real-world faults; mutants triggered only by one test's exact inputs were curbed by instructing agents to mutate logic, as two example pairs show (§5; App. A.5). The specifications are far more detailed than typical developer documentation, which the authors defend as a proxy for specifications good enough to build from while warning the evaluation may overestimate agents. Every artefact inherits the reference implementation's bugs. The scope is command-line programs in compiled languages (§5). The paper is a preprint; data and code are announced for release on publication, and coding agents built the benchmark's specifications, suites and mutants, checked by the pipeline and by hand (Reproducibility Statement; AI Usage Statement).

## Key Statistics

| Instances | 165, from 200 after filtering |
| Mutants per instance | mean 74, median 67 |
| Killed exactly by target test | 73.0% (32.4% before refinement) |
| Best M | 55.5% (Claude Opus 5); four of six agents below 40% |
| V and R, four agents | V 88-96%; R 86-93% |
| Sol reasoning effort | M 31.3% (low) to 46.5% (xhigh) |

| Opus alone vs three pooled | 54% vs 59% killed; 41% killed by none |
| Reference tests per task | 944, against 1-62 in five prior benchmarks |

## Key Connections

- An existing benchmark of 200 command-line programs: the base the instances, executables, suites and build-script approach come from [BT].
- Code-generation benchmarks that scaled from issues to whole applications, cited neutrally; one of them is Jimenez et al. (2024) [BT].
- Agent re-implementations of a C compiler and a web browser, and a claim that autonomous development depends on strong verification [BT].
- Five prior test-generation benchmarks, contrasted on scope and on providing the implementation [BT].
- Prior work on natural-language ambiguity as a source of testing errors, and on generic rule-based mutations [BT].

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Re-implementation successes do not show autonomous development of new software is near, because new software has no existing tests to verify against.
2. Valid tests are not strong tests; a high pass rate on the reference gives a false impression of well-tested software.
3. Specification ambiguity does not explain weak suites; test design does.
4. Developer-written documentation is too underspecified to generate tests from.
5. Generic rule-based mutations cannot guarantee requirement-specific faults.
